platform.label: Platform
platform.description: Ingress, identity integration, shared infrastructure, and telemetry.

backend.label: Backend
backend.description: Application services, domain logic, and asynchronous workers.

data.label: Data
data.description: Databases, caches, object storage, and schema contracts.

external.label: External Provider
external.description: Identity or third-party services outside the repository boundary.

nodes.title: Web Client
nodes.purpose: The browser client initiates user actions and renders service responses.

details.summary: A user-facing client calls the service through the public API edge and holds only presentation/session state.
what: Submits user requests over HTTPS.
Receives domain responses and error states.
why: Separates user interaction from service state and server-side authorization.
failures: Authentication redirects, stale cached assets, and network failures are the first client-side checks.

nodes.title: API Gateway
nodes.purpose: The public ingress validates requests and routes them to the application service.

details.summary: The gateway is the service boundary for TLS termination, request routing, rate policy, and identity handoff.
what: Accepts HTTPS requests.
Applies edge policy before forwarding to the service.
why: Keeps public ingress concerns out of domain service code.
failures: Check route tables, token validation policy, rate limits, and gateway logs.

nodes.title: Identity Provider
nodes.purpose: An external identity service issues and validates user identity claims.

details.summary: The identity provider is outside the service boundary but affects every authenticated request.
what: Issues login tokens.
Publishes signing keys and identity metadata.
why: Centralized identity avoids embedding credential management in the application service.
failures: Expired keys, clock skew, tenant misconfiguration, and callback URL drift commonly break auth.

nodes.title: Application Service
nodes.purpose: The core service enforces domain rules and coordinates stateful dependencies.

details.summary: The application service owns request handling, authorization decisions, domain validation, persistence coordination, and async job creation.
what: Runs domain logic.
Reads cached or durable state.
Publishes work when requests require background processing.
why: Centralizes the business contract behind one API boundary.
failures: Inspect request logs, dependency latency, schema errors, authorization branches, and queue publication failures.

nodes.title: Cache
nodes.purpose: A low-latency store keeps hot reads and derived state close to the service.

details.summary: The cache accelerates repeated reads and shields the database from avoidable hot-path load.
what: Stores short-lived values keyed by service queries.
Expires entries according to TTL or invalidation rules.
why: Improves latency while keeping durable truth in the database.
failures: Stale keys, stampedes, oversized values, and missing invalidation create hard-to-debug state drift.

nodes.title: Primary Database
nodes.purpose: Durable application state is stored behind the service contract.

details.summary: The database is the system of record for entities, transactions, and constraints that must survive restarts.
what: Stores normalized or document state.
Enforces schema and transactional constraints.
why: Separates durable truth from cache and background processing artifacts.
failures: Check migrations, lock contention, slow queries, connection pools, and backup/restore posture.

nodes.title: Job Queue
nodes.purpose: The queue buffers work that should not block the user-facing request.

details.summary: The queue decouples request latency from slower or retryable background operations.
what: Receives jobs from the application service.
Delivers jobs to workers with retry and visibility semantics.
why: Protects the request path from long-running work and transient downstream failures.
failures: Backlog growth, poison messages, retry storms, and dead-letter volume indicate async health issues.

nodes.title: Worker
nodes.purpose: Background workers consume queued jobs and update durable or external state.

details.summary: Workers execute asynchronous jobs, write results, and isolate retry-heavy work from user-facing APIs.
what: Consumes messages.
Reads and writes durable state.
Stores large artifacts when needed.
why: Keeps slow processing and retries out of the synchronous request path.
failures: Check worker concurrency, queue visibility timeout, idempotency, and dead-letter handling.

nodes.title: Object Storage
nodes.purpose: Large immutable artifacts live outside the primary transactional database.

details.summary: Object storage keeps generated files, uploads, exports, and other large artifacts referenced by database metadata.
what: Stores byte streams by key.
Returns object URLs or metadata to the service.
why: Avoids putting large binary payloads into the transactional database.
failures: Permission drift, lifecycle expiration, and orphaned metadata can break artifact reads.

nodes.title: Telemetry
nodes.purpose: Logs, metrics, and traces connect user symptoms to service and dependency behavior.

details.summary: Telemetry receives signals from client, edge, service, worker, and dependency paths for diagnosis and operations.
what: Collects logs, metrics, traces, and structured events.
Supports dashboards, alerts, and incident investigation.
why: Provides the cross-cutting view needed when failures span multiple nodes.
failures: Sampling gaps, missing correlation IDs, noisy alerts, and dropped events reduce debugging confidence.

overview.title: Service Topology Overview
overview.summary: A non-swimlane service map showing clients, public edge, domain service, stateful dependencies, async workers, artifact storage, identity, and observability.

request-path.title: Request Path
request-path.summary: The synchronous path starts at the web client, crosses the API edge, validates identity context, and reaches the service with cache and database dependencies.

async-path.title: Async Path
async-path.summary: The asynchronous path moves non-blocking work through a queue to workers that update durable state and object artifacts.

operations.title: Operations View
operations.summary: Operational signals from the edge, service, queue, and worker converge in telemetry for debugging and incident response.
